Chapter 3 • Topological Manifolds

3.3 Smooth Manifolds

  • An atlas is \(C^\infty\)-compatible, denoted as \(\mathcal{A}_{C^\infty}\), if for any pair of charts \(\left(\mathcal{U}, \mathscr{X}\right), \left(\mathcal{V}, \mathscr{Y}\right) \in \mathcal{A}_{C^\infty}\):

    1. Either \(\mathcal{U} \cap \mathcal{V} = \emptyset\), or

    2. \(\mathcal{U} \cap \mathcal{V} \neq \emptyset\) and both chart transition maps, \(\textrm{\runic ᛖ}_{\mathcal{V}\mathcal{U}}\) and \(\textrm{\runic ᛖ}_{\mathcal{U}\mathcal{V}}\), are \(C^\infty\) functions in the “ordinary multivariable calculus sense”4.

  • A \(d\)-dim. smooth manifold (or \(C^\infty\)-manifold)5 is the triple \(\left( \mathcal{M}, \mathcal{O}_\mathcal{M}, {\mathcal{A}}_{C^\infty} \right)_d\).

3.3.1 Smooth Maps and Diffeomorphisms

  • Smoothness of maps is defined through charts, by reducing it to ordinary multivariable calculus. A function \(f : \mathcal{M} \to \mathbb{R}\) on a smooth manifold \(\left( \mathcal{M}, \mathcal{O}_\mathcal{M}, \mathcal{A}_{C^\infty} \right)_d\) is smooth if, for every chart \((\mathcal{U}, \mathscr{X}) \in \mathcal{A}_{C^\infty}\), its chart representative \begin{align*} f \circ \mathscr{X}^{-1} : \mathscr{X}(\mathcal{U}) \subseteq \mathbb{R}^d \longrightarrow \mathbb{R} \end{align*} is \(C^\infty\) in the ordinary multivariable calculus sense. This is where \(C^\infty\)-compatibility becomes essential: if \(f \circ \mathscr{X}^{-1}\) is smooth and \((\mathcal{V}, \mathscr{Y})\) is another chart, then on \(\mathscr{Y}(\mathcal{U} \cap \mathcal{V})\) \begin{align*} f \circ \mathscr{Y}^{-1} = \left( f \circ \mathscr{X}^{-1} \right) \circ \left( \mathscr{X} \circ \mathscr{Y}^{-1} \right) = \left( f \circ \mathscr{X}^{-1} \right) \circ \textrm{\runic ᛖ}_{\mathcal{V}\mathcal{U}}, \end{align*} a composition of smooth maps, hence smooth. Smoothness checked in one chart around each point therefore holds in all charts: the notion is chart-independent. On a merely topological manifold, whose transition maps are only continuous, no such chart-independent notion of differentiability would exist.

  • More generally, given two smooth manifolds \(\left( \mathcal{M}, \mathcal{O}_\mathcal{M}, \mathcal{A}_\mathcal{M} \right)_{d}\) and \(\left( \mathcal{N}, \mathcal{O}_\mathcal{N}, \mathcal{A}_\mathcal{N} \right)_{e}\), a continuous map \(\phi : \mathcal{M} \to \mathcal{N}\) is smooth if, for every pair of charts \((\mathcal{U}, \mathscr{X}) \in \mathcal{A}_\mathcal{M}\) and \((\mathcal{V}, \mathscr{Y}) \in \mathcal{A}_\mathcal{N}\), its chart representative \begin{align*} \mathscr{Y} \circ \phi \circ \mathscr{X}^{-1} : \mathscr{X}\big( \mathcal{U} \cap \mathrm{preim}_\phi(\mathcal{V}) \big) \subseteq \mathbb{R}^d \longrightarrow \mathscr{Y}(\mathcal{V}) \subseteq \mathbb{R}^e \end{align*} is \(C^\infty\). Continuity of \(\phi\) guarantees that \(\mathcal{U} \cap \mathrm{preim}_\phi(\mathcal{V})\) is open, so the representative is defined on an open subset of \(\mathbb{R}^d\), and the same composition argument as above shows that the notion is chart-independent. Two special cases will be used constantly:

    • smooth functions are the smooth maps into \(\mathcal{N} = \mathbb{R}\), equipped with its standard smooth structure \(\left( \mathbb{R}, \mathcal{O}_\mathbb{R}, \{ (\mathbb{R}, \mathrm{id}_\mathbb{R}) \} \right)_1\);

    • smooth curves are the smooth maps \(\gamma : \mathbb{R} \to \mathcal{M}\), with \(\mathbb{R}\) carrying the same standard structure: \(\gamma\) is smooth if and only if \(\mathscr{X} \circ \gamma\) is \(C^\infty\) on \(\mathrm{preim}_\gamma(\mathcal{U})\) for every chart \((\mathcal{U}, \mathscr{X})\).

  • A diffeomorphism is a smooth bijection \(\phi : \mathcal{M} \to \mathcal{N}\) whose inverse \(\phi^{-1} : \mathcal{N} \to \mathcal{M}\) is also smooth. If one exists, \(\mathcal{M}\) and \(\mathcal{N}\) are diffeomorphic. Diffeomorphic manifolds are indistinguishable as smooth manifolds, just as homeomorphic spaces are indistinguishable as topological spaces, and isomorphic vector spaces as vector spaces. This is the notion of equivalence implicit in the footnote on exotic smooth structures above.

4

By “ordinary multivariable calculus sense” we mean that the transition maps, \(\textrm{\runic ᛖ}_{\mathcal{V}\mathcal{U}} \colon \mathbb{R}^d \longrightarrow \mathbb{R}^d\) and \(\textrm{\runic ᛖ}_{\mathcal{U}\mathcal{V}} \colon \mathbb{R}^d \longrightarrow \mathbb{R}^d\), are smooth functions between open subsets of \(\mathbb{R}^d\) in the usual calculus sense, i.e., they admit continuous partial derivatives of all orders.

Useful remarks:

  • Here we refer specifically to \(C^\infty\)-compatibility, but the notion of compatibility extends naturally to any desired degree of differentiability (\(C^k\), \(C^\omega\), etc.), depending on the structure one wishes to impose.

  • Whitney’s Theorem states that, for \(k \geq 1\), every maximal \(C^k\)-atlas contains a \(C^\infty\)-atlas, and that the resulting smooth structure is unique up to diffeomorphism. Hence, for \(k \geq 1\), nothing is lost by working directly with \(C^\infty\)-manifolds. For \(k = 0\) the analogous statement fails: there exist topological manifolds admitting no smooth structure at all.

5

It is important to emphasize that it is possible to define two atlases, \(\mathcal{A}_1\) and \(\mathcal{A}_2\), on the same topological space \(\left( \mathcal{M}, \mathcal{O}_{\mathcal{M}} \right)\) that are both internally \(C^\infty\)-compatible, but not compatible with each other. In other words, the union \(\mathcal{A}_1 \cup \mathcal{A}_2\) does not form a valid \(C^\infty\)-atlas because the chart transition maps between charts from \(\mathcal{A}_1\) and \(\mathcal{A}_2\) are not smooth. In that case, each atlas defines a different smooth structure on the same topological manifold. These are then regarded as two distinct smooth manifolds with the same underlying topological space but different smooth structures. This is not just a pathological possibility: there exist topological manifolds that admit multiple inequivalent smooth structures. A famous example is \(\mathbb{R}^4\), which admits uncountably many non-diffeomorphic smooth structures, known as exotic \(\mathbb{R}^4\)’s. These are topologically homeomorphic to the standard \(\mathbb{R}^4\) but not diffeomorphic to it or to each other. Another classical example is the 7-dimensional sphere \(S^7\), for which John Milnor discovered in 1956 the existence of exotic spheres, i.e., smooth structures on \(S^7\) that are not diffeomorphic to the standard round sphere. Kervaire and Milnor later showed that \(S^7\) admits exactly 28 smooth structures up to orientation-preserving diffeomorphism (15 if orientation-reversing diffeomorphisms are also allowed). For this reason, when defining a smooth manifold, one should consider not just an arbitrary \(C^\infty\)-compatible atlas but rather the entire collection of charts that are smoothly compatible with it. This ensures that the smooth structure is fully specified. If two atlases are not compatible, they belong to different maximal atlases and define distinct smooth structures on the same topological space.
